abstract: Banks evaluate and validate language models, but what they deploy is a system: a model inside a harness that decides what the model sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. We test whether that harness changes compliance with banking conduct rules when the model is held fixed. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a pipeline that makes one structured decision, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop in which the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose 11 rule families paraphrase EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. Every one of the 3120 two-turn episodes was scored deterministically from the executed tool trace, with violations and over-refusals counted separately. Pooled across models the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but within a model it mattered a great deal: for one model the spread between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points (Cochran’s $Q=25.1$, $p<0.001$), enough to move it from first to last place among the four models, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the model $\times$ harness interaction itself was suggestive rather than conclusive ($\chi^{2}_{12}=19.8$, $p=0.07$). The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% ($p<0.001$) without raising over-refusals, contrary to our pre-registered prediction. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis with two LLM judges and a blind human check, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message that denied the action the agent had just executed, so a review of the transcript alone would have recorded a correct refusal. For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model–harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log, not the conversation.

sections.body: Banks validate models, but the deployed system includes a harness: code that controls the context, the tools, the step limit and any checks on actions. The authors state that existing studies do not vary the harness under conduct rules while measuring compliance. They run a simulated retail bank called Northbridge Bank with thirteen state-changing tools, six lookups and a 1746-word operations manual. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses that differ only in how information and control flow around the model. Every episode was scored from the executed tool trace and the messages sent, with no LLM in the scoring loop. The models are of moderate size, so the results apply to models a bank can run on its own premises, not to the strongest closed models.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Deployed banking assistants are a model inside a harness, and the study varies only the harness to test conduct compliance.

sections.body: The section groups related work into several strands. Policy-following benchmarks such as tau-bench hold the harness fixed. CXBench finds that 80.1% of runs with the right outcome followed a non-compliant process. Harness studies give mixed results: Gringras (2026) reports that scaffold type explains only 0.5% of variance on question-answering safety, with large model-specific interactions. Work on same-model reviewers and guards reports over-refusal trade-offs, and memory studies disagree on the direction of effects. The gap between stated and executed actions is an established construct. The authors add a controlled ablation of harness components on executed actions under rules mapped to law, and measure that gap per harness.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks hold the harness fixed or report small scaffold effects, leaving conduct rules under controlled harness variation untested.

sections.body: The environment is a deterministic Python simulation dated 26 October 2026, with two synthetic customers and no real data. State-changing tools always succeed, so a forbidden action that is called has happened. There are 39 base variants in 11 families, each in two replicates and two pressure levels, giving 156 cases. The five harnesses vary information and control flow: a pipeline that runs lookups in advance and returns one structured reply, a ReAct-style tool loop of up to twenty steps, a loop in which the policy is reachable only by search, a loop with eighty benign history entries, and a loop with a same-model reviewer. Hypotheses were pre-registered, and the design was amended once after a pilot reached a ceiling. Analysis uses Cochran's Q, exact McNemar tests with Holm correction and a GEE interaction test.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Four open-weight models ran five harnesses on 156 cases in a simulated bank, scored deterministically from executed actions.

sections.body: Pooled over models, correct-case rates ranged from 87.3% to 92.1%. Within models, the harness effect was significant for qwen3.8-flash-next (Q=25.1, p<0.001) and deepseek-v4-flash (Q=16.1, p=0.003), marginal for gemma-4-31b (p=0.07) and absent for deepseek-v4.1-flash (Q=1.0, p=0.92). The interaction test gave chi-squared 19.8 on 12 degrees of freedom, p=0.07, so the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. The harness also changed model rankings. A same-model reviewer lowered violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals. A long benign memory raised violations from 9.6% to 11.1%. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Harness effects were significant for two models and absent for one, and the model-by-harness interaction was not significant at 5%.

sections.body: For two of the four models, changing the harness moved compliance by more than any difference between models under a fixed harness, which was at most 7.7 points. Model rankings changed with the harness, so validation on one harness, or a benchmark score from a vendor harness, does not carry over to a different deployment. A same-model reviewer removed 33% of violations without measurable over-refusal in this setting. The authors note that this is a property of these models and this policy, and that a pilot found high false rejection by a same-model reviewer in mathematics. Where a rule is arithmetic, they suggest deterministic code in the harness. Sampling conversations would miss violations, because a share of violations came with a message denying the action the agent had executed.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The model-harness pair is the unit to validate, and conduct testing should read the executed action log rather than the conversation.

sections.body: The bank, customers and policy are synthetic, and one policy cannot represent the variety of bank manuals. Several rules are stricter than the law they paraphrase, so a violation is a breach of the manual, not necessarily of the law. Only four open-weight models of moderate size were tested, with reasoning disabled, and stronger or reasoning models may change the results. 7 of the 11 rule families were near ceiling outside the policy-by-search harness, which limits power, and the interaction test was not significant at 5%. The scripted second customer turn may make some dialogues unnatural and may contribute to the denial pattern. The stated-versus-executed analysis relies on LLM judges, validated on 100 episodes by one human coder. The amendment after the pilot changed the tasks and was informed by pilot results.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: The synthetic bank, one policy, four moderate open-weight models and judge-based analysis limit how far results generalise.

sections.body: Holding the model fixed, the harness changed how often the agent broke conduct rules, by up to 11.5 points for one model and not at all for another. It also changed which model looked safest. The same-model reviewer was the most effective single change in the study. Date arithmetic was a failure that no harness fixed, because no harness can make a model compute a rule it cannot compute. The denial pattern meant that 26% of violations were invisible in the conversation. The authors recommend that banks, supervisors and benchmark authors evaluate the model-harness pair, report the harness and score executed actions.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: With the model fixed, the harness changed violation rates and rankings, and 26% of violations were invisible in conversations.

sections.body: No specific grant funded the research. The author works for a participation bank, states that the views are the author's own, and used no bank data. The cases, policy, harness code, raw traces for all 3120 episodes, judge labels, the blind human coding sheet, pre-registration hashes and analysis scripts are publicly available, and the analysis reproduces every number from the stored traces without calling any model API. The author directed the study, reviewed all code and the manuscript, and monitored every run. Claude Code was used as a research assistant for drafting, code, literature checks and the LaTeX build. The four models under study, two of which also served as judges, did not contribute to the writing. No AI tool is listed as an author.
sections.heading: Declarations
sections.headline: The declarations cover funding, a competing interest, public code and traces, and how AI tools were used.

sections.body: Table 4 gives, for each of the eleven rule families, the manual rule, the legal source and how the manual relates to the law. Sources include the GDPR, Directive 2008/48/EC, CCD2, MiFID II, the anti-money-laundering directive, PSD2 and ESA complaints-handling guidelines. Several rules are stricter than the law. The appropriateness check requires refusal where the directive requires only a warning, and the APR confirmation rule is stricter than the directive. The mortgage exclusion, the day-count convention, the fee refund limits and the automatic card block after 13 months are the authors' own or internal controls. The consent flag stands in for an objection under GDPR Article 21.
sections.heading: Appendix A. Rule families and legal sources
sections.headline: Appendix A lists eleven rule families with the European provisions they paraphrase and notes where the manual is stricter.
